recipe: n<=10: brute force over all n! permutations is fine at a one-second limit. Laaksonen's table pairs n<=10 with O(n!). Past roughly n=12, drop permutations for subset iteration.
trigger_condition: Is the input size at most about 10?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, ch.2 Estimating efficiency

recipe: n<=20: O(2^n) subset enumeration fits a one-second limit. USACO Guide stretches this to O(2^n * n) at n<=20, which is exactly the budget for bitmask DP.
trigger_condition: Is the input size at most about 20?

recipe: n between 25 and 40 with an exponential search: meet in the middle turns 2^n into 2^(n/2). Note 2^(n/2) is sqrt(2^n), a genuinely different complexity class.
trigger_condition: Is n too large for 2^n but at most 40?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Meet in the middle

recipe: n<=500 admits O(n^3) per Laaksonen; USACO Guide is stricter at n<=400. Treat 400-500 as the cubic ceiling, so Floyd-Warshall is the default all-pairs choice there.
trigger_condition: Is the input size at most about 500?

recipe: Quadratic ceiling is contested: Laaksonen says n<=5000 for O(n^2), USACO Guide says n<=7500. Both assume one second. Treat 5000 as safe, 7500 as needing good constants.
trigger_condition: Is the input size in the low thousands?

recipe: n around 10^4 to 10^5 with per-query work: O(n*sqrt(n)) is acceptable up to n<=7*10^4 per USACO Guide. That is the sqrt-decomposition and Mo's-algorithm budget.
trigger_condition: Is n near 10^5 with an sqrt-per-query algorithm?

recipe: n around 10^5: expect O(n) or O(n log n). Laaksonen notes this directly rules out quadratic, since (10^5)^2 = 10^10 operations takes tens of seconds.
trigger_condition: Is the input size about 10^5?

recipe: n up to 10^6: O(n log n) is the working ceiling. USACO Guide puts O(n log n) at n<=5*10^5 and plain O(n) at n<=5*10^6; Laaksonen allows both at 10^6.
trigger_condition: Is the input size around one million?

recipe: Values up to 10^18: only O(log n), O(log^2 n), or O(1) survive. This signals binary search, binary exponentiation, digit DP, or a closed form rather than enumeration.
trigger_condition: Does a bound in the statement exceed 10^9?

recipe: USACO Guide states the actual number: a conservative estimate is 10^8 operations per second, but it could be closer to 5*10^8 given good constant factors. A 5x spread, not a constant.
trigger_condition: Are you converting an operation count into a runtime estimate?

recipe: Laaksonen never says 10^8. The text says a modern computer can perform some hundreds of millions of operations in a second. The folklore 10^8 is the pessimistic end of that range.
trigger_condition: Are you citing an exact operations-per-second constant?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Estimating efficiency

recipe: MIT 6.006 anchors estimates differently: one operation per cycle on a 1 GHz single-core machine, so 10^9 per second. Their table gives n=1000 quadratic as 1 ms, linear as 1 microsecond.
trigger_condition: Do you need a machine-independent baseline for runtime estimates?

recipe: The thresholds are time-limit relative, not absolute. USACO's table assumes 2-4 second limits; Laaksonen's assumes one second. Rescale the table before trusting any n bound.
trigger_condition: Is the problem's time limit different from one second?

recipe: Exponential is not merely slow, it is impossible. MIT 6.006 tabulates 2^1000 at n=1000 as roughly 10^281 millennia, against fewer than 10^100 particles in the universe.
trigger_condition: Is your candidate algorithm exponential with n above 50?

recipe: Read the target complexity backwards into a shape: O(n^2) means all pairs, O(n^3) means all triplets, O(2^n) means all subsets, O(n!) means all permutations. Laaksonen's mapping.
trigger_condition: Have you derived a target complexity but not an approach?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Complexity classes

recipe: At n=20, n! is about 2.4*10^18 while 2^n is about 10^6, a twelve-order gap. Whenever a DP state can be a subset instead of a permutation prefix, take the subset.
trigger_condition: Does your brute force iterate over orderings of the input?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Bit manipulation / DP

recipe: Bitmask DP over subsets costs O(2^n * n) time and a 2^n-sized table. Memory, not time, is often the binding constraint past n=22, since the array is indexed by 1<<n.
trigger_condition: Does your DP state need a subset of at most 25 items?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, DP over subsets

recipe: Thresholds presuppose the Word-RAM: arithmetic, comparison, bitwise ops, and memory access on O(1) machine words are O(1). If your values exceed a machine word, per-op cost is no longer constant.
trigger_condition: Do the problem's values exceed 64 bits?
source_name: MIT 6.006 Spring 2020, Lecture 1: Model of Computation

recipe: MIT 6.006's working definition: efficient means polynomial time in the input size. Everything except O(2^n) and O(n!) in the standard ladder is polynomial, so k in n^k is the real question.
trigger_condition: Is your algorithm's exponent a constant independent of input?

recipe: Knapsack-style DP is O(N*W): linear in items but linear in the numeric capacity, not in its bit length. A large W blows up even when N is tiny, so bound W before choosing this.
trigger_condition: Does the DP dimension come from a value rather than a count?

recipe: n<=80 allows O(n^4) and n<=400 allows O(n^3) in USACO Guide's finer-grained table. Useful when a fourth nested loop is the natural formulation of a small-n problem.
trigger_condition: Is the input size at most about 80?

recipe: Static array, many range-sum queries: prefix sums, O(n) build then O(1) per query. In 2D the same idea gives O(NM) build with four lookups per submatrix query.
trigger_condition: Are there many range-sum queries with no updates?
source_name: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums

recipe: Point updates interleaved with range sums: Fenwick tree, O(log N) update, O(log N) query, O(N) space. Easier to code than a segment tree, especially multidimensional.
trigger_condition: Are there range-sum queries on a mutating array?

recipe: Range updates plus range queries: segment tree with lazy propagation, O(log n) each. The update must be composable so deferred updates combine, and must apply uniformly to a whole segment.
trigger_condition: Must a single update modify an entire range?

recipe: Segment trees need the combining operation to be associative with an identity element. Sum, min, max, gcd qualify. If your aggregate is not associative, a segment tree will not compose.
trigger_condition: Is the aggregate associative with an identity element?

recipe: Immutable array, range min/max/gcd: sparse table, O(N log N) build then O(1) per query. O(1) needs an idempotent operation where double-counting an overlap is harmless.
trigger_condition: Is the array immutable with idempotent range aggregates?

recipe: Sparse table on range sums degrades to O(log N) per query, since overlapping power-of-two blocks double-count. For non-idempotent aggregates prefer a Fenwick tree.
trigger_condition: Is the range aggregate a sum rather than a minimum?

recipe: Many range increments with values read only at the end: difference array. Add at l, subtract at r+1, prefix-sum once. O(M) total instead of O(M*K) naive looping.
trigger_condition: Are range increments applied before any value is read?
source_name: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums

recipe: For each element, find the nearest smaller preceding element: maintain a stack of increasing values, popping while the top is larger. Each element is pushed once and popped once, so O(n) amortized.
trigger_condition: Do you need each element's nearest smaller neighbour?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Nearest smaller elements

recipe: Minimum over a fixed-width window sliding left to right: monotonic deque. Pop from the back while larger than the incoming value, pop the front when it leaves the window. O(n) total.
trigger_condition: Is the window a fixed width moving one step at a time?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Sliding window minimum

recipe: Only the extreme element ever matters: use a heap. Insert and remove are O(log n), peek is O(1). Rust's docs frame BinaryHeap as processing only the biggest item.
trigger_condition: Do you repeatedly need only the current extreme element?
source_name: Rust std::collections, Which collection should you use

recipe: The k-th order statistic once, order of the rest irrelevant: std::nth_element partitions in O(N) average comparisons via introselect, beating a full O(N log N) sort.
trigger_condition: Do you need one order statistic without a full ordering?

recipe: Predecessor, successor, or ordered iteration needed: balanced tree map with worst-case O(log n) insert, lookup, erase. Rust's BTreeMap adds O(log n) range queries that a hash map cannot serve.
trigger_condition: Do you need keys near a query key rather than exact?

recipe: Need the rank of a key or the k-th smallest element in a dynamic set: g++ policy-based indexed_set supports find_by_order and order_of_key, both logarithmic. Ordinary std::set cannot.
trigger_condition: Do you need rank queries on a changing sorted set?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Policy-based data structures

recipe: Membership tested more than once per element with no ordering needed: hash table, expected amortized O(1) for build, find, insert. Rebuild with a fresh random hash when load factor drifts.
trigger_condition: Is membership tested repeatedly without needing key order?

recipe: Keys are small integers in a bounded universe u: direct-access array gives worst-case O(1) find, insert, delete. Cost is O(u) space, so this fails once n is far below u.
trigger_condition: Do keys fit a small dense integer range?

recipe: Incremental connectivity, merges only, no deletions: disjoint set union with path compression plus union by rank gives amortized O(alpha(n)), which never exceeds 4 for any reasonable n.
trigger_condition: Do components only ever merge, never split?

recipe: DSU also covers Kruskal cycle detection, connected components of images, online bipartiteness checking, and offline range minimum or LCA queries. Reach for it whenever grouping is monotone.
trigger_condition: Does the problem ask whether two items ended up grouped?

recipe: Detect whether any two segments intersect: sweep line over endpoint events, keeping active segments in a balanced set ordered by y at the sweep position. O(n log n); only neighbours need testing.
trigger_condition: Must you find intersecting pairs among many segments?
source_name: CP-Algorithms, Search for a pair of intersecting segments

recipe: One pattern in one text: prefix function on pattern + separator + text gives all occurrences in O(n+m) with O(n) space. Also yields the smallest period as n minus the last prefix value.
trigger_condition: Are you searching for a single fixed pattern?

recipe: Many patterns against one text: Aho-Corasick builds a trie with suffix links in O(m*k) over total pattern length, then scans in O(len + ans). Running KMP per pattern would be O(n*m).
trigger_condition: Are you matching a dictionary of patterns at once?

recipe: Repeated equality tests between arbitrary substrings: polynomial prefix hashes, O(n) precompute then O(1) per comparison, versus O(min(n1,n2)) for direct comparison.
trigger_condition: Do you compare arbitrary substring pairs many times?

recipe: Queries are all known upfront and one element can be added or dropped cheaply: Mo's algorithm reorders them by block of left endpoint, giving O((N+Q)*sqrt(N)) total.
trigger_condition: Are all range queries known before any answer is needed?
source_name: CP-Algorithms, Sqrt Decomposition and Mo's algorithm

recipe: Aggregate has no clean segment-tree merge but blocks can be summarised: sqrt decomposition into sqrt(n) blocks, O(n) preprocess, O(sqrt(n)) per query. Simpler to write than a lazy segment tree.
trigger_condition: Is the aggregate awkward to merge in a segment tree?

recipe: Non-negative weights on a sparse graph: Dijkstra with a priority queue, O(m log n). On a dense graph where m approaches n^2 the plain array version at O(n^2 + m) is preferable.
trigger_condition: Are all edge weights non-negative?

recipe: Every edge weight is 0 or 1: skip the heap entirely. 0-1 BFS with a deque, pushing weight-0 edges to the front and weight-1 to the back, runs in O(E).
trigger_condition: Is every edge weight in the set {0,1}?

recipe: Any negative edge weight present: Dijkstra is invalid. Bellman-Ford runs n-1 relaxation phases in O(nm), and one extra phase that still relaxes proves a negative cycle exists.
trigger_condition: Can any edge weight be negative?

recipe: All-pairs distances with n at most a few hundred: Floyd-Warshall, O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space. Tolerates negative edges; a negative diagonal entry reveals a negative cycle.
trigger_condition: Do you need distances between every pair of vertices?

recipe: Dependencies form a directed graph with no cycles: topological sort via DFS exit times, O(V+E). It both orders the DP and detects cycles, since no ordering exists when one is present.
trigger_condition: Does the graph have directed dependency edges without cycles?

recipe: Cycle in a successor chain under tight memory: Floyd's tortoise and hare, O(n) time and O(1) space. A visited hash set solves the same problem but costs O(n) memory.
trigger_condition: Is memory too tight to store every visited state?

recipe: Efficient insertion at both ends: deque. Python's collections.deque gives O(1) append and pop at either end, while a list's pop from the middle or front is O(n).
trigger_condition: Do you add at one end while removing at the other?

recipe: You can cheaply verify a candidate answer but not compute it: binary search the answer space. Requires a predicate that flips false to true exactly once; monotonicity is the whole precondition.
trigger_condition: Is feasibility monotone in the value you are optimising?

recipe: Cost is O(log(range)) times the cost of one check. Two common shapes: sort once then O(n) per check giving O(n log n), or search a value range bounded by the constraints.
trigger_condition: Have you confirmed a monotone predicate for the answer?

recipe: Continuous answer space: binary search on reals reaches precision delta in O(log(range/delta)) steps. Use it for root finding when no closed form exists, iterating a fixed count rather than comparing floats.
trigger_condition: Is the answer a real number rather than an integer?

recipe: Many independent binary searches over the same timeline: parallel binary search batches them, sharing each check and updating state incrementally. Turns O(N*K log K) into O((N+K) log N log K) on the Meteors problem.
trigger_condition: Do many queries each binary search the same sequence?

recipe: Positive values, target subarray sum: two pointers both moving only right. The right pointer travels O(n) steps total regardless of per-step bursts, so the whole scan is O(n).
trigger_condition: Does extending the window change the objective monotonically?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Two pointers method

recipe: 2SUM: sort, then walk one pointer right from the start and one left from the end. O(n log n) dominated by the sort. The same shape extended by one loop gives 3SUM in O(n^2).
trigger_condition: Are you searching for a pair summing to a target?

recipe: Sorting first often beats maintaining a dynamic structure. Laaksonen measured set intersection: sort-then-merge ran about ten times faster than an ordered set, despite both being O(n log n).
trigger_condition: Can the whole input be processed after one sort?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Comparison to sorting

recipe: Values span a huge range but only n distinct ones appear: sort, dedupe, replace each value by its sorted index. Indexing an array over 0..10^9 directly would simply exceed the memory limit.
trigger_condition: Are coordinate values far sparser than their numeric range?
source_name: USACO Guide, Custom Comparators and Coordinate Compression

recipe: Split the search space in half, enumerate each half, then combine. Subset-sum drops from O(2^n) to O(2^(n/2)) by building two sorted halves and matching them with a merge-like scan.
trigger_condition: Can partial results from two halves be combined cheaply?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Meet in the middle

recipe: Convert range updates into point updates: store deltas, apply +v at l and -v at r+1, and recover values with one prefix-sum pass. The inverse transform of prefix sums.
trigger_condition: Are there many range adds with queries only afterwards?
source_name: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums

recipe: Monotonic stack is the amortised-analysis pattern: each element enters and leaves once, so an inner loop that looks unbounded is O(n) overall. Recognise it by nearest-greater or nearest-smaller phrasing.
trigger_condition: Does an inner loop pop items that can never return?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Amortized analysis

recipe: Replace iteration over permutations with iteration over subsets. The elevator problem falls from O(n!*n) to O(2^n*n) by storing, per subset, the ride count plus the last group's weight.
trigger_condition: Does the optimal order depend only on the set chosen so far?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, DP over subsets

recipe: Summing over all subsets of every subset is O(2^(2n)) naively. Restricting which elements may be removed at each step (sum over subsets DP) brings it to O(2^n * n).
trigger_condition: Must you aggregate over all sub-subsets of each subset?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, DP over subsets

recipe: Both give the same complexity, states times transitions. Laaksonen notes most competitive programmers prefer the iterative loop because it is shorter with lower constant factors, while recursion is easier to reason about first.
trigger_condition: Are all DP states reachable in a simple index order?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Dynamic programming

recipe: Memoization wins when the reachable state space is far sparser than the full table, since tabulation must fill every cell. Keep recursion when transitions are irregular.
trigger_condition: Is the set of reachable states much smaller than the table?

recipe: Greedy is safe only when the locally optimal choice is provably globally optimal. Laaksonen's warning: even the simple coin problem needs a nontrivial exchange argument to justify taking the largest coin.
trigger_condition: Can you prove the local choice never blocks a better global one?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Greedy algorithms

recipe: Greedy fails on arbitrary coin sets: with coins {1,3,4} and target 6, greedy yields 4+1+1 while optimal is 3+3. One counterexample kills a greedy; DP solves the general case in O(n*k).
trigger_condition: Are the greedy choice's parameters arbitrary rather than fixed?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Greedy general case

recipe: Longest increasing subsequence: the O(n^2) DP is fine below n=5000, but maintaining tails (smallest ending value per length) and binary searching gives O(n log n). Swap the comparison for non-decreasing.
trigger_condition: Are you finding a longest monotone subsequence?

recipe: Keys are integers in 0..c with c = O(n): counting sort in O(n), escaping the comparison-model lower bound. Only works when the key can index an array directly.
trigger_condition: Are sort keys small integers usable as array indices?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Counting sort

recipe: Any associative operation raised to a large power: binary exponentiation in O(log n) multiplications. Works for modular arithmetic, matrices, and anything else satisfying associativity.
trigger_condition: Is the repeated operation associative?

recipe: Linear recurrence with an astronomically large index: encode one step as a matrix, then binary exponentiate. Fibonacci in O(log n); counting length-k paths via adjacency powers in O(n^3 log k).
trigger_condition: Does a fixed-size linear recurrence run for huge n?

recipe: Smallest period of a string: compute the prefix function, take k = n - pi[n-1]. If k divides n, k is the period; otherwise the string has no useful compression.
trigger_condition: Are you asked for a repeating unit inside a string?

recipe: Process DP states in topological order so every dependency is resolved before use. This turns an exponential recursive search into O(V+E) whenever the state graph is acyclic.
trigger_condition: Do DP dependencies form an acyclic directed graph?

recipe: USACO Guide's pragmatic rule: implement the slower correct solution first, for example O(N^2) when O(N) is optimal. It earns partial credit while giving you a reference for optimising.
trigger_condition: Is the optimal approach still unclear after analysis?

recipe: Dynamic array append is O(1) amortized but a single append that triggers growth is O(n), because everything must move. If tail latency matters, the amortized figure is the wrong one.
trigger_condition: Does a single slow operation break your latency budget?

recipe: Hash tables are expected amortized O(1), a doubly hedged claim. Python dict get, set, and delete are O(1) average but O(n) amortized worst case; cppreference gives the same for unordered_map.
trigger_condition: Does the workload depend on hash-table worst-case behaviour?

recipe: DSU with only path compression is O(log n) per query; with only union by rank it is also O(log n). The near-constant inverse Ackermann bound requires both optimisations together.
trigger_condition: Did you implement only one of the two DSU optimisations?

recipe: Hash-based average cases assume no adversary. CP-Algorithms warns that colliding strings can be generated independently of the base p, so modulus 2^64 is not recommended against adaptive tests.
trigger_condition: Could an adversary choose the inputs you hash?

recipe: Birthday paradox on hashes: one comparison collides with probability 1/m, but 10^6 mutual comparisons against m = 10^9+9 makes a collision near certain. Use two moduli to reach an effective 10^18.
trigger_condition: Are you comparing far more than sqrt(modulus) hashed items?

recipe: bisect.insort is O(n), not O(log n): the Python docs state the logarithmic search is dominated by the linear insertion step. Finding the position is cheap; making room is not.
trigger_condition: Are you inserting into an array-backed sorted list repeatedly?

recipe: std::stable_sort is O(N log N) only when its temporary buffer allocation succeeds. If allocation fails it silently falls back to O(N log^2 N). Memory pressure is a complexity risk.
trigger_condition: Is memory tight while sorting a very large range?

recipe: Python set intersection is O(min(len(s), len(t))) on average but O(len(s) * len(t)) worst case. The average figure assumes a hash function robust enough that collisions stay uncommon.
trigger_condition: Do your set elements have a weak hash function?

recipe: Same asymptotics, tenfold difference: Laaksonen measured set-based intersection at 10.0s versus sort-based at 0.9s for n=5*10^6, both O(n log n). A tree maintained throughout loses to one upfront sort.
trigger_condition: Are two candidate algorithms in the same complexity class?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Efficiency comparison

recipe: Swapping an ordered set for a hash set gave a 4-5x speedup in the same measurement, with no algorithmic change. When the ordering is unused, paying for a balanced tree is pure overhead.
trigger_condition: Are you using an ordered container without using the order?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Efficiency comparison

recipe: A priority queue and an ordered set both give logarithmic insert and remove, but the heap has smaller constants because it is far simpler than a balanced binary tree.
trigger_condition: Do you need only the extreme element, not full ordering?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Priority queue

recipe: Big-O deliberately discards constants and low-order terms. An O(n) algorithm may execute n/2 or 5n operations, a tenfold real difference that the notation is designed not to express.
trigger_condition: Are you choosing between algorithms of identical asymptotic order?

recipe: Recursion depth is a hard resource, not an asymptotic one. Python's limit exists to stop C stack overflow crashing the interpreter; the highest safe value is platform-dependent and raising it can crash.
trigger_condition: Can recursion depth grow linearly with the input size?

recipe: Sparse table buys O(1) queries with O(N log N) memory and no update support. Fenwick keeps O(N) memory and allows updates, at O(log N) per query. Choose by whether the array mutates.
trigger_condition: Does the underlying array ever change after construction?

recipe: Direct-access arrays give worst-case O(1) rather than expected O(1), paid for with O(u) space. Ten-letter name keys would need about 17.6 TB, which is why hashing exists.
trigger_condition: Is the key universe vastly larger than the item count?

recipe: The n log n sorting lower bound holds only in the comparison model, proved by a decision tree of height at least log2(n!). Counting sort evades it by not comparing elements.
trigger_condition: Does your algorithm only compare elements pairwise?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Sorting lower bound

recipe: Comparison-model search is Omega(log n) by the same decision-tree argument. Beating it requires an operation with super-constant branching, which is exactly what array indexing on a Word-RAM provides.
trigger_condition: Are you trying to beat logarithmic search by comparisons?

recipe: std::sort's guarantee changed: before LWG713 the standard allowed plain quicksort with O(N^2) worst case. The requirement is now O(N log N) worst case, which is why introsort is used.
trigger_condition: Are you relying on a library sort's worst-case bound?

recipe: std::nth_element is O(N) average comparisons, not worst case. Introselect is a hybrid; treat the linear bound as expected behaviour, unlike std::sort's hard guarantee.
trigger_condition: Do you need a hard worst-case bound on selection?

recipe: The Word-RAM charges one unit per word touched, which is virtually never true on real hardware. Modern machines move whole blocks, so an analysis ignoring blocks can mispredict real runtime badly.
trigger_condition: Does the working set exceed cache size?

recipe: Demaine's hierarchy figures: L1 about 1ns, L2 about 10ns, main memory about 150ns, disk about 10ms. Seven orders of magnitude between the ends dwarfs most constant-factor reasoning.
trigger_condition: Does the data structure spill out of main memory?

recipe: An asymptotically identical algorithm can win hugely on real input shape: Java's TimSort needs roughly n comparisons on nearly sorted arrays, far fewer than n lg n, while matching mergesort on random data.
trigger_condition: Is the input likely already partially sorted?

recipe: Scanning N items costs ceil(N/B) block transfers, and the ceiling matters: when N is smaller than a block you still pay for a whole block. Tiny operations are not free at the memory boundary.
trigger_condition: Are you doing many tiny reads scattered across memory?

recipe: Need equal elements to keep their input order: use a stable sort. std::sort explicitly does not preserve it; std::stable_sort and Python's sorted do. Java's Object sort is stable, its primitive sort is not.
trigger_condition: Must equal-key records retain their original relative order?

recipe: Stability costs memory. Java's stable object sort takes O(n/2) temporary storage on random data, dropping toward nothing as input becomes sorted. Unstable in-place sorts avoid that buffer entirely.
trigger_condition: Is the extra sort buffer affordable for this input size?

recipe: Java splits by element kind: primitives use dual-pivot quicksort for speed, objects use a stable adaptive mergesort. You rarely choose the algorithm; you choose the array type, which chooses for you.
trigger_condition: Are you sorting boxed objects rather than primitives?

recipe: Sorting by a derived value: pass a key function, not a comparator. Python's docs note the key is called exactly once per record, while a cmp-style comparator is invoked on every comparison.
trigger_condition: Is the sort key expensive to compute per element?

recipe: Do not hand-roll a sort. Laaksonen's reasoning: the library version is certainly correct, certainly efficient, and costs no implementation time. Reach for a custom sort only with a non-comparison key structure.
trigger_condition: Are you about to implement a sorting algorithm yourself?
source_name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook, Laaksonen, Sorting in C++

recipe: Hash map when you want arbitrary keys with no extra functionality, a cache, or plain lookup. Tree map when you want sorted iteration, on-demand ranges, or the largest key below a bound.
trigger_condition: Do you ever query keys by proximity rather than equality?
source_name: Rust std::collections, Which collection should you use

recipe: Latency-sensitive path: a tree map's O(log n) is worst case, while a hash map's O(1) degrades to O(n) under collisions. Pick the tree when the tail matters more than the mean.
trigger_condition: Is worst-case latency more important than average throughput?

recipe: Never depend on hash-map iteration order: cppreference states elements are not sorted in any particular order, only bucketed by hash. Sort explicitly when output order is part of the contract.
trigger_condition: Does downstream code depend on iteration order?

recipe: Known final size: call reserve or rehash upfront. Insertions that cross max_load_factor trigger a rehash that invalidates every iterator and re-buckets everything, turning a cheap loop into repeated O(n) work.
trigger_condition: Do you know roughly how many entries you will insert?

recipe: Rust's blunt default: you should probably just use Vec or HashMap. The other collections have genuinely optimal use cases, but those cases are borderline niche for generic storage and processing.
trigger_condition: Is this ordinary storage without an identified access pattern?
source_name: Rust std::collections, Which collection should you use

recipe: When complexities tie, prefer Vec over VecDeque over LinkedList. Rust's docs recommend a linked list only when you cannot tolerate amortization, need cheap splitting, or are absolutely certain.
trigger_condition: Are you considering a linked list for a sequence?

recipe: Use a heap when you store many elements but only ever process the most important one. If you also need lookup by key or ordered traversal, a heap is the wrong structure.
trigger_condition: Do you only ever consume the current best element?

recipe: Python's explicit guidance: for k equal to one use min or max; for small k use nlargest or nsmallest; for large k just call sorted and slice. No fixed crossover is specified.
trigger_condition: Are you extracting the k largest items from an iterable?

recipe: Repeated top-k extraction from the same data: convert the iterable to a heap once, then use heap operations. One O(n) heapify amortises across many O(log n) pops.
trigger_condition: Will you extract extremes from the same collection repeatedly?

recipe: Python list pop from the end is O(1) but from the middle or front is O(n), and insert is O(n). If you pop from the front in a loop, switch to collections.deque.
trigger_condition: Do you remove elements from the front of a list?

recipe: Maintaining sortedness incrementally in an array costs O(n) per insert. Either batch all insertions then sort once, or use a tree-based ordered container that inserts in O(log n).
trigger_condition: Are inserts into a sorted sequence interleaved with reads?

recipe: Data exceeds RAM: switch models. The external memory model counts block transfers between a size-M cache and unbounded disk, both in size-B blocks, and operations inside cache are free.
trigger_condition: Does the dataset exceed available main memory?
source_name: MIT 6.851 Spring 2012, Lecture 7: External Memory Model

recipe: On-disk indexes use a B-tree with branching factor about B, giving O(log_B N) transfers per search, insert, or delete. That is a factor of log B better than a binary tree, and it is optimal for search.
trigger_condition: Is the index stored on disk rather than in memory?

recipe: Sorting out of core: do not insert into a B-tree, which costs O(N log_B N) transfers. Use M/B-way mergesort for O((N/B) log_(M/B) (N/B)) transfers, which is optimal in the comparison model.
trigger_condition: Are you sorting a dataset larger than memory?

recipe: Buffer trees batch updates so the amortised cost per operation drops below one block transfer, which point-at-a-time structures can never reach. Batching is an asymptotic win at the memory boundary, not just a convenience.
trigger_condition: Can updates be accumulated before answers are required?

recipe: Buffer trees delay queries until an explicit flush, which answers everything outstanding in O((N/B) log_(M/B) (N/B)). If every query must be answered immediately, this whole family is unavailable.
trigger_condition: Must every query be answered before the next arrives?

recipe: Block size unknown, or several cache levels in play: use cache-oblivious layouts. A van Emde Boas tree layout achieves O(log_B N) transfers without the algorithm ever referring to B.
trigger_condition: Must the code run well across unknown cache configurations?
source_name: MIT 6.851 Spring 2012, Lecture 7: Cache Oblivious Model

recipe: Cache-oblivious analysis assumes an optimal offline replacement policy, which is safe in practice: LRU and FIFO are O(1)-competitive with it given twice the cache, and doubling M does not change these bounds.
trigger_condition: Are you worried the real cache policy invalidates the analysis?
source_name: MIT 6.851 Spring 2012, Lecture 7: Cache Oblivious Model

recipe: MIT 6.006's first rule of attack: reduce to a problem you already know before designing anything. Their catalogue is search structures, sorts, shortest paths; only then brute force, divide and conquer, DP, greedy.
trigger_condition: Have you tried mapping the task onto a known problem?
source_name: MIT 6.006 Spring 2020, Lecture 1: How to Solve an Algorithms Problem

recipe: Pick the interface first, then the implementation. Sequence means extrinsic position: first, last, nth. Set means intrinsic key order: queries by key. Different structures serve the same interface at different costs.
trigger_condition: Do you access items by position rather than by key?
